topics.name: iOS & Swift
topics.blurb: Swift, SwiftUI/UIKit, concurrency, memory, app lifecycle

concepts.what: In Swift, structs and enums are value types, meaning they are copied when assigned or passed. Classes are reference types, so variables refer to the same instance in memory. Value types help avoid unintended side effects and are thread-safe by default.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to check your understanding of Swift's memory model and how it affects data flow and bug prevention.
concepts.tip: I use value types for models and reference types for shared, mutable state.

concepts.what: Optionals in Swift represent values that may be absent, using `?` and `!`. Protocols define blueprints for methods and properties, supporting polymorphism and code reuse.
concepts.why: These are core Swift features; interviewers want to see if you can handle missing data safely and design flexible APIs.
concepts.tip: I always unwrap optionals safely using guard or if-let.

concepts.what: Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) manages memory for class instances. Retain cycles occur when two objects hold strong references to each other, preventing deallocation. Use `weak` or `unowned` references to break cycles, especially in closures and delegate patterns.
concepts.why: Memory leaks are a common source of bugs; interviewers want to know you can prevent them.
concepts.ex:
class A { var b: B? }
class B { weak var a: A? }
concepts.tip: I check for retain cycles in closures and delegate relationships.

concepts.what: SwiftUI uses property wrappers like `@State`, `@Binding`, and `@ObservedObject` to manage view state reactively. UIKit relies on imperative state updates and delegates. SwiftUI's approach reduces boilerplate and helps avoid inconsistencies.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you understand modern state management and can compare it to UIKit's patterns.
concepts.tip: I choose the right property wrapper based on ownership and update needs.

concepts.what: Swift 5.5+ introduces async/await for structured concurrency, making asynchronous code readable. Actors provide data isolation for shared mutable state. The `MainActor` ensures code runs on the main thread, critical for UI updates.
concepts.why: Concurrency bugs are subtle; interviewers want to know you can write safe, efficient async code.
concepts.ex:
actor Counter { var value = 0; func inc() { value += 1 } }
@MainActor func updateUI() { /*...*/ }
concepts.tip: I use actors for shared state and always update UI on the main actor.

concepts.what: iOS apps move through states: not running, inactive, active, background, and suspended. Background tasks let apps finish work when not in the foreground, using APIs like `BGTaskScheduler`.
concepts.why: Proper lifecycle handling is key for resource management and user experience.
concepts.ex: func applicationDidEnterBackground(_:) { saveData() }
concepts.tip: I handle cleanup and save state in lifecycle callbacks.

concepts.what: Networking uses URLSession for HTTP requests. Codable enables easy encoding/decoding of models to JSON. Persistence can be handled with Core Data or SwiftData for local storage of structured data.
concepts.why: These are essential for real-world apps; interviewers want to see practical data handling skills.
concepts.ex:
struct User: Codable { let name: String }
let data = try JSONEncoder().encode(User(name: "Alice"))
concepts.tip: I use Codable for safe, concise JSON parsing.

concepts.what: Unit tests in Xcode use XCTest. You can test logic, UI, and performance. Mocks and dependency injection help isolate code for reliable tests.
concepts.why: Testing ensures code quality and maintainability.
concepts.ex: func testSum() { XCTAssertEqual(sum(2,3), 5) }
concepts.tip: I write tests for critical logic and use mocks for dependencies.

concepts.what: Releasing to the App Store involves code signing, provisioning, passing App Store review, and managing versions. TestFlight is used for beta distribution.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to know you understand the full release pipeline.
concepts.ex: Increment version in Xcode, archive, upload via Organizer, submit for review.
concepts.tip: I follow Apple's guidelines and use TestFlight for pre-release testing.

qa.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class in Swift?
qa.a: Structs are value types, so they are copied when assigned or passed. Classes are reference types, so variables refer to the same instance. Also, only classes support inheritance and deinitializers.

qa.q: How do you safely unwrap an optional in Swift?
qa.a: I use `if let` or `guard let` to safely unwrap optionals, which prevents runtime crashes from nil values. For example, `if let name = user.name { print(name) }`.

qa.q: What does the `weak` keyword do?
qa.a: `weak` creates a non-owning reference to an object, preventing retain cycles. It's commonly used for delegates or back-references in closures.

qa.q: How do you make a struct conform to a protocol?
qa.a: You declare conformance in the struct's definition, like `struct Car: Drivable { ... }`, and implement the protocol's required methods and properties.

qa.q: Explain how `@State` and `@ObservedObject` work in SwiftUI.
qa.a: `@State` is used for simple, local state owned by a view. `@ObservedObject` is for referencing an external, observable object that conforms to `ObservableObject`, allowing the view to react to its changes.

qa.q: How does ARC work in Swift?
qa.a: ARC automatically manages the memory of class instances by keeping track of strong references. When an instance's reference count drops to zero, it's deallocated. Retain cycles can prevent this, so we use `weak` or `unowned` to break them.

qa.q: How do you perform a network request and decode JSON in Swift?
qa.a: I use URLSession to make the request, then decode the response using Codable and JSONDecoder. For example, I create a model conforming to Codable and call `JSONDecoder().decode(Model.self, from: data)`.

qa.q: What is the role of the MainActor in Swift concurrency?
qa.a: MainActor ensures that code runs on the main thread, which is required for UI updates. By annotating functions or classes with @MainActor, I guarantee thread safety for UI-related code.

qa.q: Describe how you would persist user data locally in an iOS app.
qa.a: For structured data, I use Core Data or SwiftData, which provide object graph management and persistence. For simpler needs, I might use UserDefaults or write Codable models to disk.

qa.q: How do you test a view model in Swift?
qa.a: I use XCTest to write unit tests for the view model's logic. I inject dependencies, use mocks for services, and assert that the view model produces the expected outputs for given inputs.

qa.q: What steps are involved in releasing an app to the App Store?
qa.a: I increment the version, archive the app in Xcode, upload it via Organizer, and submit it for review. I also use TestFlight for beta testing and ensure all assets and metadata are complete.

qa.q: How would you debug a memory leak caused by a retain cycle in a Swift app?
qa.a: I'd use Xcode's memory graph debugger to identify objects that aren't being deallocated. I look for strong reference cycles, especially in closures or delegate patterns, and refactor to use `weak` or `unowned` where appropriate.

qa.q: Compare state management in SwiftUI and UIKit for a complex form.
qa.a: In SwiftUI, I'd use @State for local fields, @ObservedObject for shared models, and @Binding for passing state down. UIKit requires manual state syncing, delegate callbacks, and more boilerplate, which increases the risk of inconsistencies.

qa.q: How would you architect a networking layer that supports async/await and is testable?
qa.a: I'd define protocols for network requests and responses, implement them using URLSession with async/await, and inject dependencies so I can mock network responses in tests. This separation makes the code modular and testable.

qa.q: Describe how you would handle background data fetches in an iOS app.
qa.a: I'd use BGTaskScheduler to schedule background fetches, ensuring I register tasks in the app's plist and handle expiration properly. I keep tasks short, update the UI when the app returns to foreground, and respect system resource limits.

qa.q: How do actors help prevent data races in Swift concurrency?
qa.a: Actors serialize access to their mutable state, so only one task can interact with their data at a time. This prevents data races and makes concurrent code safer without manual locking.

qa.q: What is Codable and how does it work?
qa.a: Codable is a protocol that combines Encodable and Decodable, allowing Swift types to be easily encoded to and decoded from formats like JSON. The compiler can automatically synthesize conformance for most structs and enums.

qa.q: What is TestFlight used for?
qa.a: TestFlight is Apple's beta testing platform. It lets you distribute pre-release versions of your app to testers before submitting to the App Store.

topics.name: Android & Kotlin
topics.blurb: Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, lifecycle, coroutines, architecture

concepts.what: Kotlin's type system distinguishes between nullable and non-nullable types, helping to prevent NullPointerExceptions at compile time. Nullable types are declared with a `?`, and safe calls (`?.`) or the Elvis operator (`?:`) are used to handle nulls safely.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can write robust code that avoids common runtime crashes due to null references.
concepts.ex:
val name: String? = getName()
val length = name?.length ?: 0
concepts.tip: I always use Kotlin's null safety features to minimize runtime crashes and make my code safer.

concepts.t: Kotlin Data Classes and Extension Functions
concepts.what: Data classes in Kotlin provide concise syntax for classes that hold data, automatically generating methods like `equals`, `hashCode`, and `copy`. Extension functions allow you to add new functions to existing classes without modifying their source code.
concepts.why: These features are core to idiomatic Kotlin and help write concise, maintainable code.
concepts.ex:
data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)
fun User.isAdmin() = id == 0
concepts.tip: I use data classes for value objects and extension functions to keep utility logic close to the types they operate on.

concepts.what: Activities and fragments in Android have well-defined lifecycle methods (`onCreate`, `onStart`, `onResume`, etc.) that manage UI and resources. Handling configuration changes, such as device rotation, is crucial to avoid memory leaks and data loss.
concepts.why: Understanding lifecycle is essential for resource management, avoiding leaks, and providing a smooth user experience.
concepts.tip: I use ViewModels to retain data across configuration changes and avoid leaking the activity context.

concepts.what: Jetpack Compose manages UI state using `@Composable` functions and state holders like `remember` and `mutableStateOf`. Recomposition happens automatically when state changes, updating only the affected parts of the UI.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can build efficient, reactive UIs using modern Android paradigms.
concepts.tip: I use Compose state APIs to ensure UI updates are predictable and efficient.

concepts.what: Kotlin coroutines enable asynchronous programming with structured concurrency, using scopes (`viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope`) to manage their lifecycle. `Flow` provides a cold, reactive stream for data, and dispatchers (`Dispatchers.IO`, `Dispatchers.Main`) control threading.
concepts.why: Concurrency and threading are critical for responsive apps; interviewers check your ability to avoid leaks and ANRs.
concepts.tip: I always launch coroutines in the appropriate scope and dispatcher to avoid memory leaks and UI freezes.

concepts.what: MVVM separates UI (View), business logic (ViewModel), and data (Repository). `ViewModel` survives configuration changes and holds UI state. Hilt is a dependency injection library that simplifies providing dependencies like repositories and use cases.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can design maintainable, testable, and scalable apps using modern architecture.
concepts.ex:
@HiltViewModel
class MyViewModel @Inject constructor(private val repo: UserRepository) : ViewModel()
concepts.tip: I use Hilt for dependency injection to keep my ViewModels and repositories decoupled and testable.

concepts.what: Room is an ORM for SQLite databases, providing type-safe access to local storage. WorkManager schedules deferrable, guaranteed background work, even if the app exits or the device restarts.
concepts.why: Persistent storage and reliable background work are common requirements in production apps.
concepts.tip: I use Room for local persistence and WorkManager for reliable background tasks that need to survive process death.

concepts.what: ANRs (Application Not Responding) occur when the main thread is blocked for over 5 seconds. Performance best practices include offloading heavy work to background threads, minimizing recompositions in Compose, and using tools like Profiler and StrictMode.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to ensure you can build responsive apps that don't freeze or lag.
concepts.ex: Coroutine launched with Dispatchers.IO for database access, avoiding blocking the main thread.
concepts.tip: I always profile my app and move expensive operations off the main thread to prevent ANRs.

qa.q: What is Kotlin null safety and how does it help?
qa.a: Kotlin null safety means that the type system differentiates between nullable and non-nullable types. This helps catch potential null pointer exceptions at compile time, making apps more robust and reducing runtime crashes.

qa.q: How do you define a data class in Kotlin and what are its benefits?
qa.a: A data class in Kotlin is declared with the `data` keyword and is used for classes that primarily hold data. It automatically generates useful methods like `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, and `copy`, making code more concise and readable.

qa.q: What is an extension function in Kotlin? Give an example.
qa.a: An extension function lets you add new functions to existing classes without modifying their source code. For example, `fun String.isEmail() = contains("@")` adds an `isEmail` method to the String class.

qa.q: What is the purpose of the `onSaveInstanceState` method in an Activity?
qa.a: `onSaveInstanceState` is used to save UI state before an Activity is destroyed, such as during a configuration change. The saved data can be restored in `onCreate` or `onRestoreInstanceState` to provide a seamless user experience.

qa.q: How does Jetpack Compose handle UI state and recomposition?
qa.a: Jetpack Compose uses state holders like `remember` and `mutableStateOf` to manage UI state. When the state changes, Compose automatically triggers recomposition, updating only the affected UI elements efficiently.

qa.q: Explain the difference between `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope`.
qa.a: `viewModelScope` is tied to the ViewModel's lifecycle and is used for launching coroutines that should survive configuration changes. `lifecycleScope` is tied to the lifecycle of an Activity or Fragment, and is suitable for UI-related coroutines that should be canceled when the lifecycle ends.

qa.q: What is a Flow in Kotlin and how is it different from LiveData?
qa.a: A Flow is a cold, asynchronous data stream that supports operators like map, filter, and can be collected in coroutines. Unlike LiveData, Flow is not tied to the Android lifecycle and is more flexible for complex data transformations and background operations.

qa.q: How does Hilt help with dependency injection in Android?
qa.a: Hilt simplifies dependency injection by automatically providing dependencies to Android components using annotations. It reduces boilerplate code, manages component lifecycles, and integrates well with ViewModels, Activities, and Fragments.

qa.q: How do you persist data locally using Room?
qa.a: Room provides an abstraction over SQLite, allowing you to define entities and DAOs for type-safe database access. You annotate data classes with `@Entity` and define queries in DAO interfaces, and Room generates the necessary code for CRUD operations.

qa.q: What is WorkManager and when would you use it?
qa.a: WorkManager is an API for scheduling deferrable, guaranteed background work that should run even if the app is killed or the device restarts. It's ideal for tasks like syncing data or uploading logs that must eventually complete.

qa.q: How do you avoid blocking the main thread in Android?
qa.a: I use coroutines or background threads to offload heavy operations like network or database access. For example, I launch coroutines with `Dispatchers.IO` for I/O tasks to keep the UI responsive and avoid ANRs.

qa.q: Describe how you would architect a feature using MVVM, ViewModel, Repository, and Hilt.
qa.a: I define a ViewModel to hold UI state and interact with a Repository, which abstracts data sources like Room or network APIs. Hilt is used to inject the Repository into the ViewModel, ensuring loose coupling and testability. The View observes state from the ViewModel, and all dependencies are provided via Hilt modules.

qa.q: How do you handle configuration changes in a Compose-based app?
qa.a: I store UI state in ViewModels, which survive configuration changes, and use Compose state APIs to bind the state to the UI. For transient UI state, I use `rememberSaveable` to persist across recompositions and configuration changes.

qa.q: What strategies do you use to prevent and diagnose ANRs in production?
qa.a: I profile the app using Android Studio Profiler and StrictMode to detect main thread violations. I ensure all expensive operations run on background threads, use WorkManager for long-running tasks, and add logging to catch slow operations in release builds.

qa.q: How would you debug a Room database migration failure in production?
qa.a: I enable Room's migration logging, write migration tests, and use fallback strategies cautiously. In production, I collect crash reports and logs, and if possible, provide a fallback migration or data export to prevent data loss while fixing the migration.

qa.q: How do you minimize unnecessary recompositions in Jetpack Compose?
qa.a: I structure my composables to be as small and stateless as possible, use `remember` and `derivedStateOf` to memoize values, and avoid passing changing parameters unless necessary. I also use tools like the Compose Layout Inspector to identify and optimize recomposition hotspots.

qa.q: How do you test ViewModel logic that uses coroutines and Flow?
qa.a: I use `runBlockingTest` or `TestCoroutineDispatcher` from kotlinx-coroutines-test to control coroutine execution in tests. For Flow, I collect emissions in tests and assert expected values, and I use dependency injection to provide mock repositories.

concepts.t: React Native Rendering: Bridge vs New Architecture
concepts.what: React Native originally used the 'bridge' to communicate between JavaScript and native code, which involved serializing messages and could create performance bottlenecks. The new architecture uses JSI (JavaScript Interface) and Fabric, enabling direct and synchronous access to native APIs, reducing latency and improving UI responsiveness. Fabric also modernizes the UI layer for better concurrency and layout performance.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you understand how rendering impacts app performance and how recent changes improve scalability and maintainability.
concepts.ex:
With the bridge:
JS thread sends a message to native thread
Native thread processes and responds asynchronously
With JSI:
JS calls native functions directly, e.g. `global.nativeFunction()`
concepts.tip: I can explain how JSI and Fabric reduce overhead compared to the legacy bridge, improving animation and UI responsiveness.

concepts.what: Expo is a managed workflow that abstracts native configuration, making it easy to build and deploy React Native apps without touching native code. The bare workflow gives full access to native files, allowing custom native modules and deeper integration but requiring manual setup and maintenance.
concepts.why: Interviewers assess your ability to choose the right workflow based on project requirements and constraints.
concepts.ex:
Expo: `expo init myApp` (no Xcode/Android Studio needed)
Bare: `npx react-native init myApp` (edit `android/` and `ios/` folders directly)
concepts.tip: I choose Expo for rapid prototyping or when native customization isn't needed, and bare workflow for advanced native integrations.

concepts.what: Navigation is handled by libraries like React Navigation or React Native Navigation, offering stack, tab, and drawer navigators. These libraries manage screen transitions, deep linking, and state persistence, crucial for user experience in mobile apps.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to know if you can architect scalable navigation flows and handle edge cases like deep links or modal stacks.
concepts.ex:
React Navigation setup:
`npm install @react-navigation/native`
`<NavigationContainer><Stack.Navigator><Stack.Screen name="Home" component={HomeScreen} /></Stack.Navigator></NavigationContainer>`
concepts.tip: I use React Navigation for flexibility and community support, and can handle deep linking and nested navigators.

concepts.what: Native modules allow JavaScript to access platform-specific features (like camera or geolocation) via custom code in Java/Kotlin (Android) or Objective-C/Swift (iOS). Permissions must be requested and handled according to platform guidelines, often using libraries like `react-native-permissions`.
concepts.why: Interviewers check your ability to bridge JS and native code and manage permissions securely and reliably.
concepts.tip: I ensure permissions are requested at runtime and handle failures gracefully, using native modules for platform-specific features.

concepts.what: FlatList optimizes rendering large lists by recycling views and rendering only visible items. Performance can degrade if items re-render unnecessarily, so using `keyExtractor`, `shouldComponentUpdate`, and `React.memo` helps minimize re-renders.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can build performant UIs and diagnose bottlenecks in list rendering.
concepts.tip: I profile FlatList with large datasets and use memoization to prevent unnecessary item re-renders.

concepts.t: OTA Updates vs App Store Releases
concepts.what: OTA (Over-The-Air) updates allow pushing JS and asset changes without app store approval, using services like Expo Updates or CodePush. Native code changes still require traditional app store releases, which involve review and longer deployment cycles.
concepts.why: Interviewers assess your understanding of deployment strategies and compliance with app store policies.
concepts.ex:
Expo OTA update:
`expo publish`
App store release:
Build APK/IPA, submit to Google Play/App Store for review
concepts.tip: I use OTA updates for bug fixes and UI tweaks, but plan app store releases for native changes or permission updates.

concepts.what: Deep linking enables apps to open specific screens from URLs or notifications, requiring navigation state to be correctly initialized. React Navigation supports deep linking via configuration and event listeners.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to know if you can integrate mobile apps with external triggers and maintain navigation consistency.
concepts.ex:
Deep link setup:
<NavigationContainer linking={{ prefixes: ['myapp://'], config: { screens: { Profile: 'user/:id' } } }} />
concepts.tip: I configure deep linking to handle URL parameters and restore navigation state reliably.

concepts.what: Fabric is React Native's new UI manager, designed for concurrent rendering and improved layout calculation. It enables faster updates and better memory management, especially for complex UIs.
concepts.why: Interviewers check if you understand how Fabric impacts UI responsiveness and future-proofing.
concepts.ex:
Fabric enables concurrent rendering:
UI updates can be scheduled without blocking the JS thread
Improved layout: Views update in batches
concepts.tip: I leverage Fabric for smoother animations and scalable UI architectures.

concepts.what: Expo provides managed APIs for updates and permissions, simplifying OTA deployments and permission handling. However, it limits access to custom native modules unless ejected to bare workflow.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can balance ease of use and flexibility when choosing Expo.
concepts.ex:
Expo OTA update:
`expo publish`
Expo permissions:
`import * as Permissions from 'expo-permissions'`
concepts.tip: I use Expo's managed APIs for rapid iteration, but switch to bare workflow for custom native features.

qa.q: How does React Native render UI components?
qa.a: React Native renders UI components by running JavaScript code that describes the UI, then communicates with native code to draw the components. Traditionally, this was done using the bridge, which sends messages between JS and native threads.

qa.q: What is Expo, and when would you use it?
qa.a: Expo is a managed workflow for React Native that simplifies setup and deployment by handling native configuration for you. I use Expo for quick prototyping or when I don't need custom native modules.

qa.q: How do you navigate between screens in a React Native app?
qa.a: I use navigation libraries like React Navigation, which provide stack, tab, and drawer navigators. These libraries manage screen transitions and navigation state.

qa.q: How do you request permissions in a React Native app?
qa.a: I use libraries like `react-native-permissions` or Expo's permissions API to request permissions at runtime, and handle the user's response to ensure the app works correctly.

qa.q: What are the main differences between Expo and bare workflow?
qa.a: Expo manages native dependencies and configuration, making development easier but limiting custom native integrations. Bare workflow gives full access to native code, allowing custom modules but requiring manual setup and maintenance.

qa.q: How does FlatList improve performance over ScrollView?
qa.a: FlatList only renders visible items and recycles views, reducing memory usage and improving performance for large lists. ScrollView renders all items at once, which can cause slowdowns with large datasets.

qa.q: How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders in FlatList?
qa.a: I use `keyExtractor` for stable keys, `extraData` to control updates, and wrap item components with `React.memo` to avoid re-rendering unless props change.

qa.q: How do OTA updates work in React Native?
qa.a: OTA updates let you push JS and asset changes directly to users without app store approval, using services like Expo Updates or CodePush. Native code changes still require app store releases.

qa.q: How do you implement deep linking in React Native?
qa.a: I configure the navigation container with a linking prop, specifying URL prefixes and screen mappings, so the app can open specific screens from URLs or notifications.

qa.q: What is JSI and how does it improve React Native performance?
qa.a: JSI (JavaScript Interface) allows direct and synchronous access to native APIs from JavaScript, reducing overhead compared to the bridge. This results in faster communication and improved UI responsiveness.

qa.q: How do you handle permissions for native modules?
qa.a: I request permissions at runtime using platform-specific APIs, check the status before accessing features, and handle denied permissions gracefully to avoid crashes.

qa.q: How would you migrate a legacy React Native app to the new architecture (JSI/Fabric)?
qa.a: I'd start by upgrading React Native to a version that supports the new architecture, refactor custom native modules to use JSI, and enable Fabric in the project configuration. I'd test UI and performance thoroughly to catch regressions.

qa.q: How do you architect navigation for a complex app with deep linking and nested flows?
qa.a: I use React Navigation with nested navigators for modular flows, configure deep linking to handle URL parameters, and persist navigation state to restore the user's position. I also handle edge cases like modal stacks and authentication redirects.

qa.q: How do you debug performance issues in FlatList with thousands of items?
qa.a: I profile rendering with tools like Flipper, check for unnecessary re-renders, optimize item components with memoization, and use `getItemLayout` for fixed-height items. I also paginate data to avoid loading too much at once.

qa.q: How do you ensure OTA updates do not break app functionality?
qa.a: I implement version checks and rollback strategies, test updates in staging environments, and avoid OTA updates for breaking changes or features requiring new permissions. I monitor update adoption and error rates after deployment.

qa.q: How would you implement a custom native module in a bare React Native app?
qa.a: I'd write platform-specific code in Java/Kotlin or Objective-C/Swift, expose it via JSI or the bridge, and register the module in the app. I'd handle permissions and lifecycle events, and write JS wrappers for easy usage.

qa.q: What are the trade-offs of using Expo OTA updates versus app store releases?
qa.a: Expo OTA updates are fast and don't require app store approval, but can't change native code or permissions. App store releases are slower but necessary for native changes and compliance with platform policies.

concepts.what: Dart's null safety feature ensures that variables can't contain null unless explicitly declared as nullable using '?'. This helps catch null reference errors at compile time rather than at runtime, making code safer and more predictable.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can write robust, error-resistant code and understand modern Dart features.
concepts.tip: I always use null safety to prevent runtime null reference errors and make my code more reliable.

concepts.what: Dart uses async/await for asynchronous programming, allowing non-blocking code execution. Isolates are Dart's way of achieving true parallelism, as each isolate has its own memory and event loop, communicating via message passing.
concepts.why: Async code and isolates are essential for responsive UIs and heavy computation in Flutter apps.
concepts.tip: I use async/await for I/O and isolates for CPU-bound tasks to keep the UI smooth.

concepts.what: Stateless widgets are immutable and don't store any state that changes over time. Stateful widgets can hold mutable state, and when that state changes, the widget rebuilds to reflect the new state.
concepts.why: Understanding widget types is fundamental to building interactive UIs in Flutter.
concepts.tip: I choose stateless widgets for static content and stateful widgets when UI needs to react to user input or data changes.

concepts.what: The `build` method describes how to display the widget in terms of other widgets. It's called whenever the widget needs to be rendered, such as after a state change.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to ensure you understand the widget lifecycle and how UI updates work.
concepts.tip: I keep my build methods fast and side-effect free to avoid unnecessary rebuilds.

concepts.what: Flutter uses three trees: the widget tree (UI structure), the element tree (widget instances and their state), and the render tree (layout and painting). Each layer has a distinct role in rendering and updating the UI efficiently.
concepts.why: A deep understanding of these trees helps with debugging, optimizing, and building custom widgets.
concepts.ex:
Widget tree: Column > Row > Text
Element tree: ColumnElement > RowElement > TextElement
Render tree: RenderColumn > RenderRow > RenderParagraph
concepts.tip: I use the Flutter DevTools inspector to visualize and debug the widget, element, and render trees.

concepts.what: State management solutions like Provider, Riverpod, and Bloc help manage and share state across widgets. Provider is simple and widely used, Riverpod offers improved testability and flexibility, and Bloc uses streams and events for predictable state transitions.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to see if you can scale apps and choose the right state management approach.
concepts.tip: I choose state management based on app complexity—Provider for simple cases, Bloc or Riverpod for larger apps.

concepts.what: Platform channels allow Flutter to communicate with native code (Kotlin/Java on Android, Swift/Objective-C on iOS) using a message-passing mechanism. This enables access to platform-specific APIs and features not available in Dart.
concepts.why: Testing your ability to integrate with native features and extend Flutter's capabilities.
concepts.tip: I use platform channels when I need to access device features not exposed by Flutter plugins.

concepts.what: Performance in Flutter means smooth UI at 60fps or higher. Jank refers to dropped frames or stuttering, often caused by expensive operations in the build or layout phases, or blocking the main isolate.
concepts.why: Interviewers want to know if you can build responsive, production-quality apps.
concepts.tip: I profile my apps with Flutter DevTools and move heavy work off the main isolate to avoid jank.

qa.q: What is null safety in Dart and why is it important?
qa.a: Null safety in Dart ensures that variables can't be null unless explicitly declared as nullable. This helps catch null reference errors at compile time, making the code safer and reducing runtime crashes.

qa.q: How do you declare an asynchronous function in Dart?
qa.a: I declare an asynchronous function using the `async` keyword, and I can use `await` inside it to wait for Futures to complete. For example: `Future<void> fetchData() async { await someAsyncCall(); }`.

qa.q: What is the difference between a StatelessWidget and a StatefulWidget?
qa.a: A StatelessWidget doesn't store any mutable state and is immutable, so it only rebuilds when its parent changes. A StatefulWidget can hold state that changes over time, and it rebuilds when that state updates.

qa.q: What does the build method do in a Flutter widget?
qa.a: The build method returns a widget tree that describes how the UI should look for that widget. It's called whenever the widget needs to be rendered or updated.

qa.q: Explain the purpose of the widget tree, element tree, and render tree in Flutter.
qa.a: The widget tree defines the UI structure, the element tree manages widget instances and their state, and the render tree handles layout and painting. These layers help Flutter efficiently update and render the UI.

qa.q: How would you manage state in a medium-sized Flutter app?
qa.a: For a medium-sized app, I often use Provider or Riverpod for state management because they're simple yet scalable. They allow me to share state across widgets and rebuild only the parts of the UI that need updating.

qa.q: How do you call native platform code from Flutter?
qa.a: I use platform channels, which let me send messages between Dart and native code. On the Dart side, I use a MethodChannel, and on the native side, I implement the corresponding handler to execute platform-specific functionality.

qa.q: What causes jank in Flutter apps and how can you avoid it?
qa.a: Jank happens when the UI can't keep up with the frame rate, often due to heavy computation or expensive widget builds on the main isolate. I avoid it by keeping build methods lightweight and moving heavy work to isolates or using compute().

qa.q: What are the advantages of using Riverpod over Provider?
qa.a: Riverpod offers better testability, improved compile-time safety, and doesn't depend on the widget tree, making it more flexible for complex apps. It also avoids some limitations of Provider, like context scoping issues.

qa.q: How does Bloc manage state in Flutter?
qa.a: Bloc uses streams and events to manage state. You dispatch events to the Bloc, which processes them and emits new states, making state transitions predictable and easy to test.

qa.q: When would you use a StatefulWidget instead of a StatelessWidget?
qa.a: I use a StatefulWidget when the UI needs to update in response to user interaction or data changes, like toggling a switch or updating a counter. StatelessWidget is better for static content.

qa.q: Describe how you would debug a performance issue (jank) in a Flutter app.
qa.a: I'd start by profiling the app with Flutter DevTools to identify dropped frames and slow widget builds. Then, I'd look for expensive operations in the build or layout phases, optimize them, and move heavy computations to isolates if needed.

qa.q: How would you design a Flutter app that needs to access a custom Bluetooth API on both Android and iOS?
qa.a: I'd define a platform channel in Dart and implement the Bluetooth logic natively in Kotlin/Java for Android and Swift/Objective-C for iOS. The Dart code would call methods via the channel and handle responses asynchronously, ensuring a consistent API across platforms.

qa.q: What are the trade-offs between Provider, Riverpod, and Bloc for state management?
qa.a: Provider is simple and great for small apps but can get messy as complexity grows. Riverpod is more robust, testable, and decoupled from the widget tree, making it suitable for larger apps. Bloc provides strict separation of concerns and predictable state but can be verbose and require more boilerplate.

qa.q: How do isolates differ from threads, and when would you use them in Flutter?
qa.a: Isolates are separate memory heaps and event loops, unlike threads that share memory. In Flutter, I'd use isolates for CPU-intensive tasks like parsing large JSON files or image processing to keep the main UI isolate responsive.

qa.q: How does Flutter ensure efficient UI updates when state changes?
qa.a: Flutter uses a combination of the widget, element, and render trees to efficiently update only the parts of the UI that changed. The framework compares old and new widget trees, updates the element tree, and only re-renders affected render objects, minimizing unnecessary work.
